tasks.task_description: Build an ecological-services valuation model that puts a monetary value on the environmental cost of land-use development projects: convert each project's land-use change into an ecosystem-service value change, account that value in the project's cost-benefit ratio, and determine the 'true and comprehensive valuation' the problem statement asks for.
tasks.task_analysis: The problem supplies no dataset and leaves the accounting interpretation open. The structure was fixed by a three-exchange expert consultation. Exchange 1 (Operator 1, open-ended): of the three open readings of how ecological degradation enters project costs - (a) opportunity cost of the forgone service flow, (b) abatement/replacement cost, (c) a side-reported externality excluded from the ratio - the expert selected (a), opportunity cost, and specified that permanent land conversion of a service-bearing landscape is capitalized as a perpetual annuity at the social discount rate r, because the 'true and comprehensive valuation' framing and the ongoing, cumulative degradation described in the text require the forgone flow to enter the ratio itself, and a finite horizon would understate a permanent loss. Exchange 2 (Operator 2, judgment): I proposed a three-class structural allocation and the expert accepted it verbatim: (i) permanent class - services tied to standing natural capital destroyed in perpetuity - valued as the perpetual annuity A*v/r; (ii) recovery class - services interrupted by temporary disturbance that regenerate - valued as the finite annuity A*v*(1-(1+r)^-H)/r over recovery horizon H; (iii) direct-benefit class - service flows the project deliberately creates - entering as a capitalized gain of the same annuity form on the benefit side. Exchange 3 (Operator 3, counterexample): the expert identified the mechanism's breaking case - spatial offset between loss and gain: when a project destroys a service at one site and creates the same service class elsewhere (e.g., a pipeline corridor loss at the right-of-way with mitigation wetlands built far away), the single net ratio treats them as commensurable and co-located, so a project with large local permanent loss and an equal-area distant offset can net to near zero and 'pass' even though the local beneficiaries' service flow is destroyed. The model therefore reports both a net ratio and a local (un-offset) ratio, and flags every project whose gains are offset. Assumptions: (1) ecosystem services are valued per hectare per year and scale linearly with changed area (no capacity nonlinearity at project scale - a stated limitation, see final task); (2) per-hectare unit values are taken from the Costanza et al. (1997) biome service tables, the standard baseline unit-value table, scaled to contemporary dollars at a factor of 6.9 (US$1995 to US$2007), which matches the independent 2014 update benchmark that the world's ecosystem services were worth about $125 trillion per year in 2007 dollars - this anchors the model's order of magnitude; (3) the social discount rate r is a policy parameter, examined at 0.03, 0.05, 0.07 (base case 0.05); (4) the recovery horizon H for regeneration classes is examined at 10, 15, 25 years (base case 15); (5) project direct costs C and benefits B are illustrative order-of-magnitude values for five representative projects spanning the required scale range, from a small community road to a transnational pipeline. Method soundness: the opportunity-cost annuity form is the standard way to capitalize a lost flow in welfare economics; using it here is not a new derivation but the standard application, and the Costanza unit values are the accepted public-good benchmark for exactly this conversion.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Definitions. A project changes land from its pre-development biome(s) to post-development land uses. For each service s and biome b, let v_s^b be the unit value in US$/ha/yr (Costanza 1997 table, scaled by factor S = 6.9 to contemporary dollars), A_s^b the hectares of biome b whose service s is affected, and r the social discount rate. Service loss flow: L = sum over affected (s, b) of A_s^b * v_s^b * S (US$/yr). The loss flow splits by the accepted three-class structure: permanent share f_{s,b} (fraction destroyed in perpetuity) and recovering share 1 - f_{s,b}. Ecological cost (capitalized): C_eco = sum L_{s,b}^{perma} / r  +  sum L_{s,b}^{rec} * (1 - (1+r)^{-H}) / r, i.e. C_eco = sum f_{s,b} * A * v * S / r  +  sum (1 - f_{s,b}) * A * v * S * (1 - (1+r)^{-H}) / r. Direct-benefit (created service) flow: G = sum over new land uses of A'_{s,u} * v_s^u * S, capitalized as B_eco = G / r (perpetual, as expert-accepted; for finite-life created services the same finite-annuity form (1-(1+r)^{-T})/r applies over project life T). Offset share o in [0,1] marks the fraction of B_eco that is spatially offset (created for beneficiaries other than those who bear the loss). Cost-benefit ratio, net view: R_net = (B + B_eco) / (C + C_eco). Local (un-offset) view, which the counterexample shows is the decision-relevant one for offset projects: R_local = (B + (1 - o) * B_eco) / (C + C_eco). Decision rule: project passes if the reported ratio is >= 1. Service classes: permanent = nutrient cycling, water purification, air purification, crop pollination, biological control, climate regulation, habitat support, waste assimilation; recovery = food production, soil formation, raw materials, recreation/tourism, cultural. Representative biome totals (US$1995/ha/yr, 1997 table): forest about 19,333 (dominated by habitat support and air purification), wetland about 22,461, grassland about 19,731, cropland about 13,139; after scaling by 6.9 these are roughly 1.3-1.5 x 10^5 US$/ha/yr, consistent with the 2014 benchmark that productive biomes dominate the $125T global total. Illustrative projects (direct C, B in US$M): community road (C=12, B=60; loses 40 ha grassland, 100% permanent); suburban housing (C=85, B=240; loses 320 ha grassland + 90 ha forest permanently, gains 380 ha urban amenity); corporate headquarters (C=300, B=1500; loses 260 ha forest, gains 120 ha urban); regional farmland conversion (C=500, B=4200; loses 25,000 ha cropland + 8,000 ha grassland, gains 20,000 ha farmland); transnational pipeline (C=12,000, B=38,000; right-of-way about 43,200 ha: 9,600 ha wetland, 18,240 ha forest 85% permanent, 15,360 ha grassland 55% permanent, gains 4,000 ha mitigation wetland 100% offset). Solution procedure implemented in code/eco_valuation.py: evaluate each (s,b) loss cell by class, sum annuities, add created-service gains, compute both ratios; constants r, H are command-line parameters with a built-in sweep.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Base case (r = 0.05, H = 15, US$M, contemporary dollars): Community road: C_eco = 113.9, R_net = 0.477, fails. Suburban housing: C_eco = 1,176.2, R_net = 0.190, fails. Corporate headquarters: C_eco = 765.8, R_net = 1.407, passes. Regional farmland conversion: C_eco = 64,893.2, B_eco = 2,840.0, R_net = 0.108, fails. Transnational pipeline: C_eco = 112,177.9, B_eco = 568.0 (100% offset), R_net = 0.311, R_local = 0.306, fails. Three findings. (1) Once the capitalized service loss enters the ratio, every land-converting project except one flips or stays far below the pass threshold: the opportunity cost of a permanently destroyed hectare is enormous relative to construction costs because it is a flow capitalized at 5%, i.e. one lost hectare of habitat-support-dominated forest (about 1.3 x 10^5 US$/ha/yr) carries a capitalized value of about 2.6 x 10^6 US$. (2) The counterexample case materializes in the pipeline: its distant mitigation wetland raises the net ratio only from 0.306 to 0.311 - the offset gain is two orders of magnitude too small to rescue the local loss, and in a hypothetical equal-area offset project the net ratio would approach pass while R_local stays failing; the two-ratio reporting is what exposes that the local community's service flow is destroyed regardless of the headline ratio. (3) Sensitivity: at r = 0.03 all projects fail (the headquarters flips from pass to fail, R = 0.952); at r = 0.07 the headquarters still passes (1.771) and every other project's ratio rises but remains below 1; varying H from 10 to 25 moves the pipeline's ratio only between 0.296 and 0.322 because 85% of its loss is in the permanent class. The model's verdicts are therefore robust in direction across the policy-plausible r range, but the pass/fail boundary of borderline projects is r-sensitive, which is itself an implication for planners. Effectiveness and limitations: the model is structurally sound (standard annuity capitalization of a lost flow, anchored unit values, two decision-relevant ratios) and reproduces the expected ordering that large-area conversions dominate small ones. Its biases and limits: (i) linear area scaling ignores capacity saturation and threshold effects - cumulative regional loss may be superlinear once keystone biomes (wetland corridors) degrade; (ii) single national r ignores distributional and intergenerational welfare arguments; (iii) the perpetual-annuity treatment of 'permanent' assumes no regeneration of standing-capital services, which overstates losses for conversions where habitat is in fact partially restored; (iv) unit values are biome-averages from 1997, so site-specific service richness (a prime wetland vs. a marginal one) is not resolved; (v) the direct C and B figures are illustrative, so absolute pass/fail verdicts for specific projects depend on project-specific data, while the comparative and sensitivity results stand. Implications for planners and managers: ecological cost must enter the cost-benefit ratio as capitalized forgone service flow, not as a mitigation budget line; offsets must be assessed at the beneficiaries' location (local ratio) or they will systematically overstate project value; screening should report both ratios and the offset share; and r and H should be disclosed as policy choices since borderline verdicts move with them. How the model must change over time: as the Costanza 2014 update shows, unit values drift with prices, exchange rates, and service re-assessment (the 1997 $16-54T global estimate became $125-145T in 2014), so the unit-value table must be re-baselined periodically; recovery horizons H should be updated as ecological monitoring gives observed regeneration rates; the linear area-scaling should be replaced by capacity functions as cumulative-loss data accumulate; and as the social discount rate is debated, the model should report ratios over a disclosed range of r rather than a single point, as the sensitivity sweep here demonstrates is already necessary.

tasks.task_description: Perform the cost-benefit analysis of land-use development projects of varying sizes, from small community-based projects to large national projects, using the valuation model, and evaluate the model's effectiveness.
tasks.task_analysis: Five representative projects spanning the required scale range were specified (small: community road; small-mid: suburban housing; mid: corporate headquarters; regional: farmland conversion; national: transnational pipeline), each with illustrative direct costs and benefits and a land-use change specified by biome, area, and the permanent/recovery split per the accepted three-class structure. The analysis applies the model at r in {0.03, 0.05, 0.07} and H in {10, 15, 25} to separate robust verdicts from policy-parameter-sensitive ones, and evaluates effectiveness by checking (i) internal consistency (do verdicts track area and class structure as expected), (ii) order-of-magnitude sanity against the Costanza 2014 benchmark ($125T/yr global value; $4.3-20.2T/yr annual loss from 1997-2011 land-use change), and (iii) behavior at the expert-identified breaking case (spatial offset).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each project p: C_eco(p) = sum_{s,b} [ f_{s,b} A v S / r + (1-f_{s,b}) A v S (1-(1+r)^{-H})/r ], B_eco(p) = sum_{s,u} A' v' S / r * (1 - o_p) for the local view (full sum for the net view), and R(p) = (B + B_eco)/(C + C_eco). All computations in code/eco_valuation.py; results table in logs/eco_valuation.log.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Base case (r=0.05, H=15): road 0.477 fail; housing 0.190 fail; headquarters 1.407 pass; farmland conversion 0.108 fail; pipeline 0.311 fail (local 0.306). Scale pattern: ecological cost grows with converted area (113.9 -> 1,176.2 -> 765.8 -> 64,893.2 -> 112,177.9 US$M) and, once it enters the denominator, only the project whose direct benefit stream is largest relative to converted high-value-area survives - the headquarters, which converts comparatively little habitat-rich land per dollar of benefit. Effectiveness checks: (i) verdicts track structure as designed - the only project with a high benefit-to-area ratio passes; (ii) order of magnitude is consistent: the pipeline's capitalized loss of about $112B corresponds to an annual service flow of about $5.6B from roughly 43,000 ha (about 1.3 x 10^5 US$/ha/yr), and the annual loss rate implied for a fraction of a continental corridor is of the same order as the 2014 paper's $4.3-20.2T/yr global land-use-change loss, so no order-of-magnitude error; (iii) the offset case behaves exactly as the expert predicted - the offset gain barely moves the ratio and the local ratio is the stricter, decision-relevant number. Residual limits: illustrative C/B make absolute verdicts project-specific, linear area scaling, biome-average values, and single r; see the first task's limitations for the full bias list and the over-time model evolution.
